answers.label: Benefits and challenges of consequential methods
answers.text: The largest risk is that consequential accounting methods are mixed with inventory accounting methods, or that reporting companies could opt to use either method for reporting scope 2 emissions. Consequential accounting is useful for strategic target setting and policy work, but not for producing meaningful physical GHG accounting results that are comparable and allocation ‘ownership’ of emissions to a particular entity. Attributional inventory accounting must be the mandatory basis of scope 2 reporting, to ensure companies and governments have as accurate as possible a ledger to track the relationship between an entity's historical emissions and claimed hypothetical emissions reductions beyond their inventory boundaries.

answers.label: Appropriateness of the TWG subgroup formula
Why the formula is or is not appropriate
answers.text: Short-Run Marginal Emissions Rates fail to capture system changes - which is the purported purpose of the consequential method. While theoretically useful to support decision-making, expert literature documents numerous examples where shortcomings in data and methods leads to erroneous estimates. Intervention impacts in reality vary by intervention and region, marginal emissions rates don’t automatically capture additionality assessments when determining avoided emissions impacts and short-run rates fail to capture structural changes which play out over years, rather than a single transition point.

answers.label: Why secondary effects should be excluded
answers.text: Lack of accurate, comparable, short-term data from year to year makes it challenging to consider secondary effects at the standard required by an accounting framework that prioritises scientific integrity and the principles of accuracy, completeness, consistency, relevance, and transparency. Incorporating SRMEs into Scope 2 while limitations to methods and data remain would open serious loopholes for corporations, allowing them to overstate the impact of projects within their annual emissions reporting. This increases the risk that reporting becomes divorced from the very real emissions in the atmosphere. This would expose companies using the GHGP to the types of legal risk faced by companies currently using consequential reporting methods to claim offsets and insets within their inventory reporting and sustainability claims. Given problems with comparability of data project to project in the consequential method, including secondary impacts into primary scope 2 reporting would also undermine the value of reporting for investors, making a company's exposure to climate risk more difficult to evaluate clearly.
